fishdesc.riverfishing.arapaima: Three metres of armour-plated Amazon that has to surface for air — watch for the roll, then put the bait where it went down. Livebait and the heaviest gear you own; it jumps like a tarpon and weighs four times more.
fishdesc.riverfishing.beluga: The Tsar-Fish herself: half a tonne of sturgeon that runs the sea and climbs the big rivers to spawn. Bottom tackle rated for a boat anchor, livebait, and a night with nothing else planned.
fishdesc.riverfishing.piraiba: The Amazon's own catfish, and the one the river stories are about — it hunts the deep channel after dark. Heavy ledger, livebait or a cut strip, and a leader, because it swallows.
fishdesc.riverfishing.goliath_grouper: A third of a tonne of reef that decided to eat your bait. The whole fight is the first ten seconds: stop it reaching the hole it lives in, or you are pulling on a rock with your line inside it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bull_shark: The one shark that swims UP the river — brackish, fresh, it does not care, which is why it turns up where no shark should be. Wire trace, the heaviest drag you own, and no hands in the water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.frilled_shark: A living fossil with three hundred backward-curving teeth, hauled up out of water that never sees the sun. Deep drops at night off a boat; most anglers never see one.
fishdesc.riverfishing.golden_dorado: The river tiger of South America: gold scales, a bulldog jaw and a habit of clearing the water three times per fight. Wobblers and spoons on a wire trace — it bites through everything else.
fishdesc.riverfishing.golden_crucian: The round bronze crucian of farm ponds — it survives water that kills everything else, freezing included. Float rod, worm or bread, and patience for the fussiest bite in the pond.
fishdesc.riverfishing.gorchak: A thumb-length carp cousin that lays its eggs inside living mussels. Bitter enough that nobody eats it — smallest hook you own, one bloodworm, shallow water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.verkhovka: A silver sliver living in the top foot of any pond, puddle or ditch — the first fish most anglers ever caught. A crumb of bread on the smallest hook, right under the surface.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sculpin: A flat-headed bottom-sitter that hides under stones in cold clean streams — find one and the water is healthy. Worm on the gravel at dusk; it does not chase, it ambushes.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tubenose_goby: The little goby with nostrils like two short tubes, at home anywhere from a river mouth to brackish shallows. Worm on the bottom, tiny hook, and it hooks itself.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kutum: A Caspian roach that grew up: brackish water, a spring run into the rivers, and a mouth built for shellfish. Fish it on the bottom with worm or bloodworm where the river meets the sea — and give it more line than a roach deserves, because eight kilos of one does not fight like a roach.
fishdesc.riverfishing.naked_carp: A carp that never put its scales on — bare skin end to end, and the same appetite as the rest of the family. Boilies on the bottom, a carp rod, and patience: it grows past twenty kilos and uses every one of them.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mullet: A grey shoal fish of harbours, estuaries and the surf line: it grazes algae and scraps off the bottom and takes bread the way a carp does. Light float tackle, a small hook and a slow drift down the current — it reaches eight kilos and fights every one of them like a fish twice the size.
fishdesc.riverfishing.anglerfish: All mouth and no manners: it lies on the deep bottom with a lure of its own dangling over its head and swallows whatever comes to look. Nothing artificial interests it — livebait or a strip of fish on the seabed, at night, in water deep enough to be dark. It does not fight so much as refuse to come up.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_marlin: The heaviest of the billfish and the fastest thing in the open sea. Troll a giant spoon, an octopus jig or a big jointed body over deep blue water and hold on: seven hundred kilos of it exists, and the strongest line the shop sells is barely enough.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blobfish: A sack of jelly from the cold deep, famous for what the surface does to its face. It waits on the bottom for something edible to drift past, and behaves the same way on a hook: a soft take, no run, no head-shake, and a curiosity in the keepnet nobody will believe.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluefin_tuna: Warm-blooded, four hundred kilos, and built like a torpedo. It takes livebait, a big swimbait or a trolled spoon, then goes straight down with the drag screaming — the fish every reel in the shop was designed against.
fishdesc.riverfishing.loach: The weather fish: a finger of a fish that lies in the mud of ponds and swamps and starts fidgeting hours before a storm. Bloodworm or a piece of worm on the bottom after dark, on the lightest tackle you own — and the best livebait a pike ever saw.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whale_shark: Twenty tonnes of shark that eats plankton. It has no interest in anything on a hook, so the only way to meet one is to chum the warm deep heavily and wait — for a very long time. It will not fight you; it will simply keep swimming, and no tackle on earth stops that.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nelma: A whitefish that turned predator: silver, deep-bodied, up to thirty kilos, hunting smelt in the cold rivers of the north. A spoon or a heavy spinner worked fast, or livebait — best in autumn, when it runs upriver to spawn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ocean_sunfish: A tonne of fish that is mostly head, drifting on its side at the surface to warm up between dives after jellyfish. Offer it something soft and translucent — an octopus jig, a soft plastic — and expect no fight at all: it is simply very, very heavy.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pollock: The cold northern shoals, in numbers no other sea fish here matches. Drop a jig or a blade down to the shoal and lift: fifteen kilos is the very top end, a kilo and a half is most days, and dinner is every single time.
fishdesc.riverfishing.red_piranha: A shoal fish the size of your hand with a bite that goes through monofilament like scissors — fish it on a leader or lose the hook on the first take. A strip of fish, liver or livebait in warm jungle water, in daylight, wherever the shoal is holding.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tiger_shark: The rubbish bin of the sea, and eight hundred kilos of it. It hunts the shallows at night and eats anything that smells: a strip of fish or livebait on the bottom, a wire leader, and a drag you have already checked twice.
fishdesc.riverfishing.linear_carp: A carp wearing a single row of big scales along the lateral line and nothing else. It is not a species: it is one allele — a scaled carp that also carries the nude gene. Cross it with a mirror and the row disappears in half the fry; cross two leather carp and a quarter of the eggs never develop at all. Boilies on the bottom, a carp rod, patience.
legendary.riverfishing.halibut.credit: Dedicated to idkwho0457_07869 — for the Florida species and a long list of bugs found
fishdesc.riverfishing.peacock_bass: A tropical bully of warm canals, and the reason local anglers carry spare tackle. Wobblers, poppers and cranks; it hits like a torpedo and keeps going.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bullseye_snakehead: An air-breathing ambusher of weedy canals, marked with the eyespot it is named for. Livebait and soft plastics: one furious run, then it gives up surprisingly fast.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mayan_cichlid: A small barred cichlid of warm shallows, bold out of all proportion to its size. Worm, maggot or bloodworm on a light float rig.
fishdesc.riverfishing.oscar: A heavy-bodied dark cichlid with orange marbling and a false eye on the tail. Worm and livebait; a stubborn, short-range scrap.
fishdesc.riverfishing.striped_bass: Seven dark stripes down a silver flank; runs the surf and the estuaries, and tolerates cold. Livebait, cut bait and spoons — a bulldog that simply does not stop.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluefish: A savage pack hunter of the coast — a mouthful of teeth that goes through mono. Spoons and castmasters, and use a leader.
fishdesc.riverfishing.jack_crevalle: Called canal tuna where it swims, and the byword for a fish that will not quit. Poppers and spoons; expect to lose the first three fights.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tarpon: The silver king: a hundred kilos of chrome scales that answers the hook by leaving the water. Livebait on the heaviest gear you own.
fishdesc.riverfishing.snook: The hard black lateral line gives it away. Lives against structure in warm inshore water and runs straight back into it — win the first seconds or lose the fish.

guide.riverfishing.waiting.title: The wait: float & bottom
guide.riverfishing.waiting.text:
A float or bottom rod is NOT retrieved. Cast once, then leave it alone and watch.
• Any RMB while you wait REELS THE CAST IN — it is not a crank. That one habit costs you a whole cast.
• No bite sound, no "Bite!" text. The float plunging or the rod tip moving is the entire cue.
• RMB only once a fish has taken — that is the strike.
• A bottom rod can sit on a rod pod and wait for you.
Only a lure rod is worked with clicks — see "Working the lure".
guide.riverfishing.drag.title: The drag
guide.riverfishing.drag.text:
Three drag positions in a fight:
• Cranking (RMB) — locked: you gain, tension climbs.
• Not cranking — working: tension bleeds slowly.
• Crouching — OPEN: the spool slips. Tension drops 3× faster and the line cannot snap — but clicks gain NOTHING, and a running fish takes line.
Open the drag on jumps and runs you cannot hold. You only gain standing up.
guide.riverfishing.stress.title: Tackle stress
guide.riverfishing.stress.text:
Overload no longer snaps the line instantly: past the limit every tick rolls a break chance that grows with the overshoot and the time held.
Ease off and the stress recovers. Surviving the abuse still frays the line.
The break message names the load in kg — match your tackle to the fish.
guide.riverfishing.livebait.title: Live bait
guide.riverfishing.livebait.text:
A fish under 150 g becomes live bait: craft it — or hold the fish, a hook in the offhand, sneak and use.
Live bait keeps the baitfish's weight: a big bait culls small takers and calls a predator ~6× its weight.
A livebait bottom rod can wait on a rod pod.
guide.riverfishing.groundbait.title: Groundbait 1: the base
guide.riverfishing.groundbait.text:
There is ONE groundbait: BASE GROUNDBAIT. Wheat seeds + bread makes two of it, and the fisherman sells it.

You can feed a spot with the base on its own and it works — it just is not very effective. It sits dead centre: neutral grind, neutral richness, nothing it is especially for. Everything after that is what you ADD to it.

## MAKING A MIX
• Put BASE GROUNDBAIT in a crafting grid together with UP TO 8 other things. The base is required — corn and boilies on their own are not groundbait, they are what you add to groundbait.
• One SLOT is one item. A stack of 64 in a slot still counts as one, because one per slot is what the craft takes.
• You get one groundbait out for every EDIBLE item in. Ballast — groundbait soil, clay — gives nothing back.
• A mix you made yourself is finished groundbait and cannot go back in the grid. Plain base can. That is what makes it the base.

## BALLAST IS THE IMPORTANT ONE
Soil and clay bring bulk, cloud and colour and no calories at all, so they are how you make a mix leaner without making it worse.

## VANILLA IS A REAL SHELF
Wheat, bread, a potato and a beetroot are hour-one items, and over the base they mix into something that genuinely fishes. You do not have to wait on a corn farm to start feeding.
guide.riverfishing.feeding.title: Groundbait 3: feeding
guide.riverfishing.feeding.text:
Right-click water to feed a 3x3 spot. A fed spot bites up to twice as fast and cuts up to 40% off the wait. The centre column counts full, the outer ring at 60%.

## YOU CANNOT OVERFEED
Throw as much as you like: more feed is more fish, and no swim ever gets worse for being fed. How STRONG it can get is capped by what is in the mix, never by how much of it.

## THE SAME RECIPE ADDS UP
A DIFFERENT ONE TAKES THE SWIM OVER — the old bed does not blend into the new one, it is simply gone, and you are told at the moment it happens. Decide the blend in the grid, not by throwing four different ones in one after another. A dye does not make a mix different.

A feeder, flat feeder, carp or 3-hook cage empties one per cast AT THE BOBBER — the landing spot, not the water in front of your boots. It is the same fed spot a right-click makes, so a cage and a hand build one swim between them.

## HOW LONG IT LASTS
3 to 12 minutes, by fraction. Dust halves every 90 seconds and washes out; whole grain halves every four and a half minutes and lies where it landed. That difference is what carries a long bottom session.

Fish over the spot and nothing takes? It is never the amount. It is the grind, the richness, or the menu.
guide.riverfishing.gbnumbers.title: Groundbait 2: the numbers
guide.riverfishing.gbnumbers.text:
Nutrition and fraction are the average over everything in the mix, weighted by how many of each and ballast included. That is how ballast dilutes: it averages in zeros.

Four things then decide how well the bed of feed fishes FOR A GIVEN SPECIES.

## FRACTION — the grind
A BIG FRACTION CALLS BIG FISH: dust for bleak and roach, whole grain and boilies for bream and carp. This is the honest answer to "why do I only catch tiddlers" — it is a choice, not a bug. Over a coarse bed the size roll also flattens, so the fish that come roll bigger. A better chance, never a promise.

## NUTRITION — how much food is down there, and how much this species wants
A carp wants a table laid; a bleak wants a cloud, and the table put down for the carp is not what it came for. This is why "just use boilies" fails: boilies are the richest and coarsest thing there is, which makes them perfect for a carp and useless for a roach.

## THE MENU — what is actually in it
If a fish eats worm, chopped worm in the feed works; its own page lists what it takes. The base and the ballast say nothing either way, which is why plain base is neither the right food nor the wrong food.

## VARIETY — and here is the part people miss
TWO numbers decide a swim:
• the SCORE, from the four above — WHO comes.
• the CEILING, from nutrition and variety — HOW MANY come. Plain base tops out at 0.48 of full pull; the base plus four rich things reaches 1.00.
A mix of three can score a perfect 1.00 and still lose to a mix of five at 0.90, because the five-part swim holds more fish. Aim for the BASE PLUS THREE OR FOUR things.

Feeding more reaches the ceiling faster. It never raises it.
guide.riverfishing.gbrecipes.title: Groundbait 4: recipes
guide.riverfishing.gbrecipes.text:
Ready recipes are a FLOOR, NOT A CEILING. Each was found by searching the pantry and checked against the fish it names — and each is beatable by somebody who tunes it for the water in front of them.

Numbers are how many of each go in the grid. Every recipe starts with the base, because that is the rule.

## HOUR ONE, no farm yet
  Base 3 + Wheat 2 + Bread 3 + Potato 1

## BLEAK, ROACH, RUFFE, GUDGEON — also winter and hard-fished water
  Base 1 + Maggot 1 + Bloodworm 1 + Wheat Seeds 3

## BREAM, white bream, blue bream, vimba, sabrefish
  Base 1 + Maggot 3 + Worm 1 + Wheat Seeds 2

## TENCH, crucian carp, ide
  Base 2 + Dough 2 + Maggot 2 + Corn 1

## CARP, mirror carp, wild carp
  Base 1 + Corn 3 + Boilie 3 + Pea 2

## GRASS CARP, silver carp
  Base 1 + Corn 3 + Pearl Barley 3 + Boilie 1

## CATFISH, eel, burbot
  Base 2 + Boilie 1 + Worm 3 + Chicken Liver 3

## STURGEON, channel catfish
  Base 1 + Boilie 1 + Worm 1 + Chicken Liver 3

## STERLET, nase — the plain worm swim
  Base 1 + Clay Ball 1 + Worm 3

## COD, flounder, conger, saithe
  Base 1 + Raw Fish Fillet 3 + Dried Kelp 1

The bream mix scores a perfect 1.00 on all five of its fish, because their grind, appetite and bait lists agree. The sterlet mix scores 1.00 too but holds a thin swim — only three things in it, one of them clay. Add a fourth edible one when you want a crowd rather than a sniper.
guide.riverfishing.community.title: Every water is its own
guide.riverfishing.community.text:
Each water has its own population: some species simply DON'T live here, while 1-3 are its signature fish — they bite half again as eagerly.
A small pond is species-poor, a big river or lake is rich. On big water the fish hold in patches — find the productive holes and banks.
The fish finder shows the spot's real population plus a "Known for:" line.
The ubiquitous smalls (rotan, roach, perch, bleak) live everywhere — no water is ever dead.
Missing a species? STOCK the water. The better the water suits it and the BIGGER the released fish, the higher the chance it settles for good; barely-livable water is single-digit odds, and even outright wrong water keeps a sliver of a chance. A species settled outside its element lives at quarter strength — but it lives.
Stock builds by weight: a trophy counts as three ordinary fish, fry count for almost nothing. Natives fatten up to 250% bite, transplants to 150%; an over-packed school (>125%) thins a quarter faster.
A failed settle is not a wasted fish: while the stock lasts, the transplant is TEMPORARILY catchable here, and disperses only if the species never takes hold.
Release your trophies — sport fishing is what feeds a water.
guide.riverfishing.lurework.title: Working the lure
guide.riverfishing.lurework.text:
The retrieve is RMB CLICKS: each click is one crank, the lure comes toward the bank.
• Wobbler & crankbait: swim only at a STEADY rhythm (a click every half-second or so). Break it and the action dies — fish follow and turn away.
• Spinner, spoon, jig, silicone: forgive almost any pace — just keep it moving.
• Topwater: click with PAUSES — every pop after a pause calls fish up from below.
Holding RMB cranks too fast: line comes in, but no fish takes that "action".
A lure left dead in the water gets no strikes.
guide.riverfishing.topwater.title: Topwater
guide.riverfishing.topwater.text:
Work the popper in a rhythm: short reel — pause — reel again. Every pop after a pause calls the fish; constant cranking drags it under.
A boil swells behind the lure before the strike, and the strike blows up the surface.
The hook-set window is short — be ready.
guide.riverfishing.trolling.title: Trolling
guide.riverfishing.trolling.text:
An assembled trolling rod (or sea spinner) in hand + a boat + three seconds of steady speed — and the line goes out behind the stern by itself.
Hold the speed: too slow sinks the lure, too fast spooks the fish.
The lure trails behind the boat for as long as you like — no need to wind it in.
No strike needed either: the boat's own pull sets the hook. Fish on — stop and fight it.
The pelagics (mahi, wahoo, tuna, marlin) live over deep water only.
guide.riverfishing.biggame.title: Sea giants
guide.riverfishing.biggame.text:
Tuna sounds: during the dive it TAKES line — do not force it, pump it back between dives.
Marlin and sailfish jump: never reel through a jump — open the drag and ride it out, or the hook rips free.
The toothy (shark, wahoo, barracuda) demand a steel or titanium leader.
guide.riverfishing.legendary.title: Legendary fish
guide.riverfishing.legendary.text:
Some species hide ONE named specimen per server — from the Queen of the Snags to the Megalodon.
The catch is announced to everyone and written into the server's history forever.
There will never be another.
guide.riverfishing.market.title: Market and the daily order
guide.riverfishing.market.text:
The fisherman's prices are alive: the more of a species the server sells, the cheaper it gets (down to −50%). The market recovers in a couple of days.
Every day he names an ORDER OF THE DAY — that species pays ×2.5, market be damned.

guide.riverfishing.spook.title: The fish notice you before they notice the bait
guide.riverfishing.spook.text:
Every fishing spot remembers a short fright. It is NOT the long depletion of a swim — it lasts 30 to 90 seconds and then it is gone.
What frightens it: running and jumping on the bank within about 6 blocks, standing IN the water, breaking a block nearby, a boat that is under way, your own shadow across the water when the sun is low behind you — and the cast itself, where the tackle lands.
While the fish are frightened the bites stop and the visible fish leave. Watch the water: the rings running outward are the fish telling you.
There is exactly one answer and it is the real one — walk in, crouch, and stand still. Crouched and motionless you make no noise at all.
This is what a long cast is FOR: what you do on the bank does not reach out there, and the only thing that frightens the fish at the far end is the splash of your own tackle landing.
Murky and deep water forgets you in half a minute; clear shallows and a small pond stay wary for a minute and a half.
guide.riverfishing.coop.title: Fishing together
guide.riverfishing.coop.text:
Everyone nearby sees the fight — the boss bar is shared with spectators within 12 blocks.
A friend can NET your fish: empty hand, crouch right beside you when the fish is nearly in.
It counts for both — the helper earns journal XP.
guide.riverfishing.thanks.title: Thanks
guide.riverfishing.thanks.text:
This mod is written by one person, but almost nothing in it was thought up alone.
38raspberry and Gabbi helped build it directly — hands on the work itself, not advice from the side. A great deal of what you are fishing with exists because of them.
And the features below are here because a player asked for them by name:
idkwho0457_07869 — the Florida nine, the whole Amazon (arapaima, piraiba, golden dorado), the bull shark and the goliath grouper. A third of the species list, effectively.
Colin_Brittan — a commercial fisherman in real life: the frilled shark and the beluga, which now stands at the very top of the level ladder.
белебобик — the sculpin and the tubenose goby, and the biome bug behind them.
vptareo-aao — splitting the crucian into silver and golden, and the electrofisher: a way to remove a nuisance species from one particular water.
Dmitriy_Smile — more freshwater fish, especially the carp family.
arsen_501 — the line, hook and rig ladder being something you actually choose between.
oneshot — the setting that stops the visible fish spawning as entities.
If something here is missing, or is wrong, say so on the Discord. That is how every line above got in.

fishdesc.riverfishing.bream: A deep-bodied shoaling bottom fish. Holds in pits and drop-offs, feeds off the bottom. Feeder or float with groundbait; worm, maggot, grain.
fishdesc.riverfishing.crucian_carp: A hardy fish of weedy ponds and backwaters. Shy; bites best in warm weather. Float, thin line, dough, worm or grain.
fishdesc.riverfishing.roach: The most common silver fish around. Bites almost everywhere, year-round. Float with a small hook; maggot, bloodworm, dough.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rudd: Bright red fins; likes the upper layers near weed. Takes mid-water. Float; dough, maggot, a pinch of bread.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_bream: Like a bream but smaller and more silver. Shoaling, bottom-dwelling. Feeder or float; worm, maggot, groundbait.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp: A strong, wary fish of warm waters that fights hard. Carp rod, strong line, boilies and corn, and always groundbait.
fishdesc.riverfishing.catfish: The largest freshwater predator, a nocturnal bottom hunter of deep pits. Ledger with a leader; livebait or big bait, at night and in warmth.
fishdesc.riverfishing.perch: A striped predator that shoals near snags and drop-offs and bites boldly. Spinning with a small spinner or soft plastic, or float with a worm.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pike: A toothy ambush predator of reeds and snags. Spinning with wobblers and spoons; always a leader; best in cold water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.zander: A nocturnal predator of deep drop-offs and sandy bottoms. Bites at dusk and night. Spinning with soft plastic or a wobbler and a leader; livebait.
fishdesc.riverfishing.gudgeon: A small bottom fish of clean sandy riffles, and great livebait. Float near the bottom, small hook, bloodworm or worm.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ruffe: A small spiny bottom-dweller, active even at night. Grabs worm and bloodworm off the bottom; often a nuisance when after bigger fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bleak: A tiny shoaling fish of the upper layers, always near the surface. Light float mid-water; maggot, breadcrumb; good livebait.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ide: A big, strong silver fish, omnivorous and wary. Holds in pits and current. Feeder and float; worm, dough, greens; also takes lures.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chub: A wary fish of fast rivers, omnivorous and will grab fry. Float and spinning; insects, bread, small spinners.
fishdesc.riverfishing.asp: A fast open-water river predator that smashes fry at the surface. Spinning, long casts, heavy spoons; strong and wary.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tench: A dark, slimy fish of weedy warm waters, feeding in the silt. Float and ledger; worm, corn; bites at dawn in warmth.
fishdesc.riverfishing.burbot: The only freshwater cod, a cold-lover active at night and in winter. Ledger on the bottom; livebait or cut fish; best in late autumn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.eel: A snake-like nocturnal fish that buries in silt by day. Ledger on the bottom; lobworm or livebait; strong tackle - it fights hard.
fishdesc.riverfishing.grayling: A handsome fish of cold clear rivers with a tall fin, holding in the current. Light tackle; insects, small spinners; needs cold water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.trout: A predator of cold fast rivers and streams; wary and strong. Spinning with small spinners and wobblers; clean cold water only.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sterlet: A small sturgeon with rows of bony scutes, feeding on the bottom in current. Ledger, worm; rare and prized - a collector's trophy.
fishdesc.riverfishing.wild_carp: The wild ancestor of the carp - a powerful, angry fighter of pits and snags. Carp tackle, the strongest line, boilies and corn; a hard fight.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mirror_carp: A carp with large, sparse mirror scales. Behaves like a carp, a touch calmer. Carp rod, boilies, corn, groundbait.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_kohaku: An ornamental carp: white body with crimson patches. A collectible caught by chance on carp tackle, more so near cherry blossom. Eating it is silly.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_tancho_sa: A koi with a single crimson spot on the head, like a tancho crane. A rare collectible; takes carp tackle near cherry groves.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_showa_san: A black koi with red and white markings. A collectible caught on carp tackle, more often in cherry biomes.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_asagi: A blue-grey netted back with red flanks. A collectible koi, a chance catch on carp tackle near cherry blossom.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_bekko: A solid-colour koi with black tortoiseshell spots. A rare collectible caught on carp tackle in cherry biomes.
fishdesc.riverfishing.grass_carp: The grass carp — a torpedo-shaped plant-eating giant of quiet water. Corn and peas over groundbait near the weeds; its run goes like a torpedo.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill: A feisty little American sunfish of ponds and bays. Takes anything alive — worm, maggot, small soft plastics; a joy on ultralight tackle.
fishdesc.riverfishing.largemouth_bass: The star of sport fishing. An ambusher of snags and weed: wobblers, soft plastics, topwater; a furious, jumping fight.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rainbow_trout: A leaping beauty of cold rivers. Spinners, wobblers and castmasters over the riffles; jump after jump on the way in.
fishdesc.riverfishing.channel_catfish: A whiskered dweller of warm rivers. Night bottom fishing: liver and worm; fights meaner and longer than its weight.
fishdesc.riverfishing.silver_carp: A plankton-filtering giant of calm water. Holds under a cloud of powder groundbait; powerful, skittish — thin line decides.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sabrefish: A silver sabre of open water. Schooling surface fishing: maggot up top, small lures; takes on the drop.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_bream: The bream's bluish schooling cousin from deep current. Feeder and float: bloodworm, maggot; best at dawn and dusk.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mackerel: A striped schooling sprinter of the sea. Castmaster and small lures on a fast retrieve; comes right inshore in summer.
fishdesc.riverfishing.herring: The eternal silver wanderer. Light sea tackle, cut bait and small lures; where there's one, there's a hundred.
fishdesc.riverfishing.garfish: An arrow with a needle beak and green bones. Small lures run high near the surface; give it a pause before striking.
fishdesc.riverfishing.seabass: The surf hunter. Shore spinning: wobblers and soft plastics in the waves; loves dusk and rolling water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.flounder: A flat master of sand-bottom camouflage. Bottom rigs from boat or shore: cut bait and worms; a shy, pressing bite.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cod: A cold-water bottom predator. Sea bottom rigs and boat jigging over depth: cut bait, soft plastics; a stubborn, steady pull.
fishdesc.riverfishing.saithe: A schooling swimmer over the drop-offs. Jigs and lures in mid-water; fast-moving, greedy takes.
fishdesc.riverfishing.conger: The conger — a night serpent of rocky drop-offs. Bottom rig with cut fish; pull the moment it takes or it rocks you up.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ray: A flat ghost of the sandy bottom. Heavy bottom rig with cut bait; feels like lifting a slab of the seabed.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mahi: Mahi-mahi — a golden-green bolt of the warm pelagic. Trolling and sea spinning near the surface; flashes every colour when it jumps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.wahoo: A striped sprinter pushing 100 km/h. Fast trolling over depth; the first run burns the drag — just hold on.
fishdesc.riverfishing.yellowfin_tuna: The freight train of the pelagic, sickle fins and all. Trolling and cut bait; it sounds without pause — pump it back between dives.
fishdesc.riverfishing.barracuda: A toothy torpedo of warm coastal water. Lures and soft plastics on a fast retrieve; a steel leader is mandatory.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_marlin: The king of the open ocean. Trolling over the abyss only; chains of jumps that tear tackle apart — fight it off an open drag. Somewhere out there swims the Leviathan.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sailfish: The fastest fish on the planet under a huge sail. Surface trolling; a cascade of jumps is its calling card.
fishdesc.riverfishing.swordfish: A loner of the deep pelagic. Trolling over the abyss; it slashes the lure with its sword first, then takes — don't rush the strike.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mako: The mako — the fastest predator in the ocean. Big-game trolling: livebait and cut fish; man-high jumps. Old-timers whisper about the Megalodon.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rotan: The rotan — a greedy head with fins, at home in any puddle or swamp. Takes anything that moves; every angler's first teacher.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nase: The river's stone-scraper, feeding in the current. Float and feeder: maggot, bloodworm; a careful daytime bite.
fishdesc.riverfishing.vimba: The vimba — the bream's migratory cousin. Runs the rivers in spring: feeder in the current, worm and maggot; a sharp, pulling bite.
fishdesc.riverfishing.smelt: A winter guest that smells of fresh cucumber. Ice and a jig: bloodworm, cut bait; find the school under the hole and it's a bucket by noon.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whitefish: A noble whitefish of cold lakes. Ice jigging and a light feeder: bloodworm; wary, soft-lipped — don't force it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.char: The Arctic char — an orange-bellied dweller of icy water. Spinners and spoons in the cold; don't look for it in warm country.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lenok: The lenok — the taimen's golden little brother. Taiga riffles at dawn: wobbler, spinner; wary, and strong to the very end.
fishdesc.riverfishing.taimen: The taimen — the red tail of the taiga, master of remote rivers. A surface mouse at dawn, big wobblers; leader mandatory, a fight with no compromise.
fishdesc.riverfishing.salmon: The Atlantic salmon — queen of its kind. Runs the rivers in autumn: spoons and wobblers against the current; jumps and runs that will not be stopped.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pink_salmon: The summer-running pink salmon of sea and river mouths. Spoons and spinners; the humpbacked males fight desperately.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sturgeon: An ancient night giant of the big rivers. Heavy bottom tackle: liver, worms; a fight measured in hours. Legends speak of the Tsar-Fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.halibut: A deep-sea flatfish colossus of a quarter tonne. Heavy boat bottom rigs: cut bait, livebait; comes up like an anchor, fighting every metre.
fishdesc.riverfishing.common_dace: A small silver fish of fast, clean riffles — it holds in the current and takes on the drop. Light float or ultralight: maggot, worm; sharp jerky runs that die out quickly.
fishdesc.riverfishing.volga_zander: The zander's smaller cousin, at home in the deep river channels. Light jigging: soft plastics, livebait; it presses to the bottom in short hard lunges, then gives up near the surface.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_eye_bream: A big-eyed bream relative of the deep current, feeding over sand and shell beds. Feeder on the channel edge: worm, maggot; it turns side-on to the flow, then tires fast.
fishdesc.riverfishing.round_goby: A stubby, big-headed bottom fish of stony ground — at home in rivers and brackish shallows alike. A simple bottom rig: worm, cut bait; it jerks hard, bolts for the rocks, then comes in like a stone.

guide.riverfishing.tacklebench.title: Tackle bench
guide.riverfishing.tacklebench.text:
The fisherman's stall ties custom tackle.
• Pick a FORM (peaceful rigs / predator lures), then the WEIGHT — heavier flies farther and costs more iron (1 ingot per 30 g), but must fit the rod's test window.
• Pick the HOOK in the FIRST WELL — click its left half for a smaller hook, its right half for a bigger one, No.16 down to No.1. You never bring one: the bench ties it on and bills the size in iron, three nuggets to the ingot. A No.16 adds one ingot, a No.4 three, and the 3-hook rig pays for all three.
• Materials: iron and string; dye is optional on lures.
• Advanced: the hook link (rigs) and the balance (lures) are written onto the tackle.
• Rigs come with the hooks pre-slotted; every piece carries its maker's name.

guide.riverfishing.cull.title: The electrofisher: taking out and putting in
guide.riverfishing.cull.text:
The electrofisher changes what a water holds: it takes a species out for good, and it puts in one that was never there. It is a tool for whoever runs the world, not for fishing: it is craftable nowhere and refuses to fire outside creative. Real electrofishing does exactly this job — a crew stuns a stretch of river, removes what does not belong and releases what does.

Right-click water for every species in the mod, laid out by family. Families down the left, one family's fish on the right — and the first category is not a family but THIS WATER, holding what lives here. The coloured strip on a row is its standing: green lives here, red was removed, grey can be put in.

Clicking a row selects it and turns it into a question; a second click on the same row does it. One click is deliberately not enough: a mis-click that empties a lake is not a mistake anyone should be able to make.

## ANY FISH, ANY WATER
There are no gates — it is an admin item, and a marlin goes into a pond if that is what you want. It simply will not be at home there: a species living outside its element sits at a quarter of full activity, present and catchable and never comfortable. That quarter is the whole cost.

## MIND THE SCOPE
A water here is a region of roughly 128 blocks, not the pond you are looking at. Clear roach from one bank and they are gone from the whole region, and a river with several bays is one water. The screen prints the coordinates the region was measured from.

The ban applies everywhere at once: the fish stops biting, vanishes from the shoal you can see in the water, drops off the fish finder and will no longer settle when stocked. That is one check rather than four, so they cannot drift apart. Putting a fish in is the same check from the other side — the species becomes a permanent resident of the region.

Reversible both ways. A struck-through fish comes back on a second click, where you removed it. Releasing one of that species in the water lifts the ban too: a fish you can see swimming has to be catchable.

guide.riverfishing.tacklebox.title: Where the tackle lives
guide.riverfishing.tacklebox.text:
Seventeen line diameters, nine hook sizes, four rig types and dozens of baits, all living loose next to your food and your building blocks. The box takes them.

Tackle only: line, hooks, rigs, lures, bait and leaders. Not rods and reels — those are what you hold, not what you rummage for.

Four sizes: 9, 18, 27 and 36 slots. Each is a craft of the one below, and a chest is the heart of every recipe.

Right-click to set it down, and it faces you. Sneak + right-click to open it, in your hand or already placed: it is the same object either way, so contents, name and colour are shared. Break it and it drops with everything still inside.

Rename it in the top row of the box itself — no anvil. Dye the inserts with any dye, like leather armour, and the contents come through the craft untouched. Four boxes with four names and four colours IS the navigation: pike, carp, winter.

The fisherman sells ready-made kits — float, pike, carp and saltwater — each named, dyed and packed with bench-graded tackle. A kit is the answer to “what do I need for pike”, in a form you can carry.
guide.riverfishing.keepnet.title: The keepnet: shape decides the room
guide.riverfishing.keepnet.text:
A keepnet is not a chest. A fish takes up room in the shape it actually is: a metre of pike lies as a long strip, a bream of the same weight as a short wide blob. Room in the net is something you solve, not something you fill.

The shape comes from length and condition. One cell is 25 cm of fish, so a 40 cm perch takes two, a metre of zander four, and a three-metre catfish hits the ceiling at seven. Width comes from Fulton's condition factor: at the same length a carp is fatter than an asp, and the grid shows it. Big streamlined fish lose their corner cells — the nose and tail taper.

Four sizes: 5×3, 7×4, 8×5 and 9×6, each crafted from the one below.

Controls: right-click the held net to open it. With a fish on the cursor, R turns it on its side. Shift-click drops a fish wherever it fits best. TIDY repacks the whole net from scratch, biggest and most awkward first — the room you think you have lost is usually there. EMPTY tips the catch into your inventory.

Fish from this mod only — no tackle, no blocks, no food. Tackle has a box of its own.

The fisherman sells them: small at level three, medium and large at four, huge at five.

guide.riverfishing.icefishing.title: Ice fishing
guide.riverfishing.icefishing.text:
A winter rod is not cast. At all. Point it at open water and it tells you so — it fishes straight down, through a hole, and nowhere else.

## THE AUGER
Right-click ice with it: ordinary, packed, blue or frosted, as long as there is WATER UNDERNEATH. That gives you a hole, and costs the auger one point of its 64.

A hole is as slippery as the ice it was cut in, it MELTS IN BRIGHT LIGHT the way ice does, and breaking it leaves water behind, never ice. Cut it where it will last.

## A HOLE IS WINTER
While you fish one, the engine treats the season as winter whatever the calendar says. Find ice in July and the fish under it behave as if it were January — which is the whole reason the burbot and the smelt below are worth walking to.

## WORKING IT
The first right-click drops the mormyshka in. Every one after that jigs it. A STEADY rhythm — one jig every 0.4 to 1.0 s — pulls the bite 34 ticks closer. Ragged or lazy jigging pulls it 8. Four times the difference, and while you are waiting it is the only thing you control.

## THE NOD
There is no bite sound and no "Bite!" text. The nod twitches, and that is the cue. Strike as you would on any other rod.

Almost nothing snags. A line hanging straight down in a hole has far less to catch on than one thrown across a lake.

guide.riverfishing.nets.title: Nets
guide.riverfishing.nets.text:
A rod takes one fish, and it takes the one that was hungry. A net takes everything at once: the fish you wanted, the fish you did not, and the brood that would have spawned next spring. Drag a seine through a pond in March and there is no April in it — that water is empty for years, not for an evening.

## WHY ANGLERS ARE NOT ALLOWED ONE
This is the whole reason nets are banned for anglers, everywhere, and why in this mod a haul from water you did not stock is poaching. The haul still happens — a net that did not work would teach nothing. But every fisherman within earshot saw it go in: the trust the contracts run on drops by five, and the water is emptied TWICE as fast as the fish you took would account for, because the brood went with them.

## WHOSE WATER IT IS
A net is a tool for a fish farmer on his own pond. Water you stocked yourself — a pair released and settled, or fry you put in — is yours to harvest, and there the net is exactly what it is for: the seine hauls one to three fish a minute, the cast net one every fifteen seconds, and each fish comes up as a plain fish with no catch card, because it was not caught. Both tools wear out.

Everywhere else, take the rod.

fishdesc.riverfishing.koi_carp:
An ornamental carp bred for its colours: white ground, red hi, black sumi, and the named varieties every keeper trades in — kohaku, sanke, showa, bekko, asagi, hi utsuri, karasu, and the two you will not find wild, platinum and tancho. Caught by chance on carp tackle, far more often by blossom; the rest are bred in a tank.
kohaku  W_ R_ bb — red on white
taisho sanke  W_ R_ B_ — red and black on white
showa  ww R_ B_ — red and white on black
bekko  W_ rr B_ — black patches on white
asagi  ww rr B_ — a blue-grey net over a dark body
platinum  W_ rr bb — plain white
hi utsuri  ww R_ bb — red on black
karasu  ww rr bb — plain black
tancho  WW RR bb — one red crown — pure at the white AND the red
